name: Moroccan Arabic
confidence_why: Boudlal 2001 describes Casablanca Moroccan Arabic with stress on a heavy final syllable and otherwise on the penult in citation forms (final in connected speech), but the controlled acoustic study of Bruggeman, Louriz, Almbark and Hellmuth 2021 found no acoustic trace of that stress and concludes the language most likely has no lexical stress, a view Maas 2019 reaches independently from corpus and pitch data and Hellmuth 2020 endorses, so the disagreement is about the type of system, with the weight of recent instrumental evidence on the no-stress side even though Bruggeman and colleagues themselves say further evidence is needed and Hellmuth and Pearce 2020 still call the status of stress disputed. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Bruggeman 2021.

sweep_summary: Four title-hits searched for moro1292 (catalog: 'descriptions disagree', Boudlal 2001 quantity-sensitive final-if-heavy-else-penult vs Bruggeman et al. 2020 no lexical stress). None yielded a readable new stress statement. (1) Schönherr 1997 is a German conversation-analysis dissertation (DNB subjects Deutsch/Gesprochene Sprache; Glottolog itself flags the ary tag as a computerized assignment from 'Interaktion'): irrelevant, drop from the moro1292 bibliography. (2) Mourchid 1997 (Perspectives on Arabic Linguistics X, pp. 283-292, doi 10.1075/cilt.153.18mou) is on-topic by title but closed (no abstract, Unpaywall closed, not cited by any of the field's reviewers we hold): medium priority, library. (3) Angoujard & El-Mejjad 1988 is really 'Aspects prosodiques du parler de Marrakech', ZAL 18: 7-32 (JSTOR, citation-only; HathiTrust search-only); the first-page snippet concerns verb-form syllabic structure, relevance to stress unclear; medium priority since El Mejjad's 1985 Marrakech thesis sits in the 'has word stress' camp per Maas 2013. (4) Benkirane 2003 (Languages and Linguistics 12: 1-12) abstract obtained from the journal's site: it is about vowel lengthening in CVC sequences, silent on stress placement, bears only on the CVC weight question; low priority. Best first-hand statement actually read this search of works with stress in the title is Maas 2019 Skript §3.4.2 (already held by the project, not a works with stress in the title), which states MA has no lexically fixed word stress and that citation-form 'stress' is utterance intonation; it corroborates the Bruggeman side of the recorded conflict and does not supersede the catalog's deciding sources. Crossref, Unpaywall, DNB SRU, Glottolog, HathiTrust API, JSTOR search (via r.jina.ai) and Bing (via r.jina.ai) were used instead

new_statements.quote: 3.4.2.1. Dabei ist die Akzentuierung eine der Schwellen bei der Analyse des MA: auf dieses wird die prosodische Struktur der europäischen Sprachen ... projiziert: mit einem lexikalisch festen Wortakzent, der im Äußerungszusammenhang durch die Profilierung eines Satzakzents ggf. „deakzentuiert" wird. Davon kann im MA nicht die Rede sein ... 3.4.2.3. Im MA ist die Akzentuierung (die prominente Profilierung in der Syllabierung) ein Exponent der Intonation. Anders als im Deutschen ist das Wort im MA nur schwach konturiert. Allerdings operieren auch viele sprachwissenschaftliche Darstellungen bei Beschreibungen des MA mit Wortakzenten. Sie sind in der Regel gestützt auf Einzelwortabfragen und übersehen, daß isoliert gesprochene Wörter vollständige Äußerungen mit einer Äußerungskontur sind.
new_statements.translation: 3.4.2.1. Accentuation is one of the thresholds in the analysis of MA: the prosodic structure of the European languages ... is projected onto it: a lexically fixed word stress which, in the utterance, is 'de-accented' where a sentence accent is profiled. There can be no question of that in MA ... 3.4.2.3. In MA, accentuation (prominent profiling in syllabification) is an exponent of intonation. Unlike in German, the word in MA is only weakly contoured. Many linguistic descriptions of MA nevertheless operate with word stresses. They generally rest on single-word elicitation and overlook that words spoken in isolation are complete utterances with an utterance contour.

new_statements.reading: Maas, first-hand (corpus + acoustic, F0/intensity), holds that Moroccan Arabic has no lexically fixed word stress: prominence is intonational and utterance-level, and the final/penult 'stress' reported from citation forms is the default falling utterance contour on an isolated word. This is the 'no word stress' side of the conflict the catalog already records; it corroborates Bruggeman et al. 2020 (who cite Maas 2013/2019) and argues against Boudlal's isolation-form rule.

new_statements.quote: To return to the question of what, if any, stress generalisation might hold in MA, currently there is no concrete evidence from any diagnostic of stress (acoustic correlates, native speaker judgments, phonological rules, etc.) that support an interpretation in favour of MA having a stress-by-position system, or in fact in favour of any other interpretation of stress assignment. Thus, the present null results are likely to accurately reflect a situation in which MA lacks lexical stress altogether. [p.21:] While these null findings do not provide conclusive evidence in favour of the absence of lexical stress in MA, they are very much compatible with it.

new_statements.relation_note: Same conclusion as the existing Maas 2019 statement (no lexically fixed word stress; prominence is utterance-level/intonational) and the same side of the 'descriptions disagree' the catalog V7 ruling already records for moro1292 (Boudlal 2001 weight-sensitive isolation rule vs Bruggeman et al. no lexical stress; catalog rule field left empty as DISPUTED). This work is the acoustic primary for the 'no word stress' side and explicitly contradicts the Boudlal/Benkirane weight-sensitive penult/final rule (the ROSTER 'fullscan' exit 'weight-sensitive' from Boudlal 2001). The catalog ruling quoted it second-hand; the quotes above are now verified against the opened file with AAM page numbers.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Instrumental study (24 Casablanca speakers, target words in carrier sentences inside scripted mock dialogues, so lexical stress is separated from phrase-level prominence). It tests the most widely held rule, 'the penultimate syllable of a word is stressed, unless the final syllable is heavy, in which case stress is final (Benkirane 1998, Boudlal 2001)' (p.21), and finds that none of f0, duration, spectral Centre of Gravity or vowel quality differs by presumed stress status, for any syllable pair, speaker, or speaker group; a side check of /a/ in word-initial vs word-final CV syllables (Figure 8, p.20) also shows no enhancement of final syllables, i.e. no support for fixed final stress either. The authors conclude the null results 'are likely to accurately reflect a situation in which MA lacks lexical stress altogether' (p.20), while hedging that null results are not conclusive (p.21). Prominence in MA is treated as postlexical/intonational: Boudlal's final 'stress' on isolation forms is reread as 'a continuation rise or list intonation' (p.6), and Mitchell 1993:202 is cited that the place of prominence in a word in isolation is not carried over to the phrase.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no secondary stress claim; the paper questions the existence of primary word stress).
new_statements.exceptions: None as such. §2.4.1 (pp.5-6) reviews the competing positions: weight-sensitive penult/final (Benkirane 1998, Nejmi 1993, Boudlal 2001), fixed final ('final prominence', Watson 2011), fixed penult (Benhallam 1989), variable pre-penultimate (El Hadri 1993), Boudlal 2001:99 isolation-vs-context split, and the no-word-stress camp (Stumme & Socin 1894, Brockelmann 1908, Fischer 1917, Cantineau 1960, Durand 1994, Aguadé 2008, per Maas 2013). §2.4.2 (p.6): native-speaker stress judgments are inconsistent (e.g. limun 'oranges' judged initial by 23 and final by 11 subjects in Boudlal 2001).
new_statements.identity_note: Bruggeman et al. 2021 describes Casablanca Moroccan Arabic specifically ('in this article it refers specifically to the Moroccan variety spoken in Casablanca', AAM p.3); speakers were 24 Université Hassan II students, 12 with Moroccan Arabic as sole home language and 12 Moroccan Arabic-Tashlhiyt Berber bilinguals (§3.1, p.8), with no group difference found. Same variety as Boudlal 2001 (Casablanca), so the conflict is not a dialect difference.

readall_conflicts: The one work opened (Bruggeman et al. 2021, JIPA, AAM pp.20-21) concludes that Moroccan Arabic most likely lacks lexical stress and that reported 'stress' (final on isolation forms, penult/final by weight) is postlexical intonation; this agrees with the existing Maas 2019 statement and with the 'no word stress' camp Maas 2013 lists (Stumme & Socin 1894, Brockelmann 1908, Fischer 1917, Cantineau 1960, Durand 1994, Aguadé 2008). It contradicts the catalog's other primary, Boudlal 2001 (ROA-650, Casablanca MA: 'stress falls on the ultimate syllable if it is heavy; otherwise on the penultimate' in isolation, final in context), and Benkirane 1998 (same weight-sensitive rule), which the catalog already records as DISPUTED/'descriptions disagree' with an empty rule field. Bruggeman et al. themselves hedge that null results are not conclusive and that a different stress rule could in principle survive, so the field-level status per this source is 'no consensus'; but every diagnostic they review (acoustics, native judgments, pitch accent alignment) fails to support any word-stress rule.

sources.quote: Stress does not produce semantic differences in Moroccan Arabic. Primary stress may fall either on the final syllable (terminal) or on the second from the last (penultimate). This is predictable on the basis of syllable structure. Stress is terminal if the last syllable of the word has the structure [CVC] or [CəCC], e.g. mskin [məskín] poor, frhan [fərhán] happy, mhlul [məhlúl] open (m), samht [səmə́ht] I forgave, sawbt [sawə́bt] I fixed (something), sllmt [səllə́mt] I greeted. Stress is penultimate if the last syllable of the word has the structure [CV] or if it ends in [-əC], e.g. sllmna [səllə́mna] we greeted, mhlula [məhlúla] open (f), kllm [kə́lləm] he talked (with, to), sahba [sáhba] girl friend. Also notice stress shift with the suffixation of pronominal suffixes, e.g. klina [klína] we ate, klinah [klináh] we ate it (m), kllm [kə́lləm] he talked (to), kllmni [kəllə́mni] he talked to me.
sources.locator: Part One Phonology, section 7.1 Stress, printed p. 29; index entry 'stress, 29'; [CəCC] is read from the examples samht, sawbt, sllmt
sources.note: Catalog kind is no-word-stress (from Bruggeman et al. 2021, instrumental). Abdel-Massih states that Moroccan Arabic has predictable, non-contrastive primary word stress: final when the last syllable is CVC or CəCC, otherwise penultimate (last syllable CV or CəC); stress shifts rightward under pronominal suffixation. This is an impressionistic pedagogical description with no measurement, so it is the traditional account that the catalog's instrumental source tested, not an instrumental counter-finding. sources.quote: 'Exceptions to the general rule of predictable stress in Arabic include Nubi ... and Moroccan Arabic, in which the status of stress is disputed. Maas and Procházka (2012) ... argue that MA - like MB - has post-lexical phrasal accentuation only, and no stress. There have been differing views on MA stress (Maas 2013), since a stress generalisation can be formulated for citation forms which no longer holds in connected speech (Boudlal 2001). One suggestion is that MA has stress but is an edge-marking language ... (Burdin et al. 2014).'

sources.quote: In a monosyllabic word, the syllable receives one primary stress. In mutlisyllabic words, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, and secondary stress falls on the final syllable. We will use 1 to indicate primary stress, 2 to mark secondary stress and 3 to indicate tertiary stress: 13) kta1 bi2 (my book) / ma 3 ga1 na2 (watch) / xdda1 ma2 (workers) / fla1 ye2k (boats)

sources.note: The catalog codes Moroccan Arabic as no-word-stress (after Bruggeman et al. 2021). This grammar states a word-stress system: primary stress on the penultimate, secondary on the final, tertiary on the first of quadrisyllables (p. 8: 'In quadrisyllabic words, tertiary stress falls on the first, secondary stress on the final syllable and primary stress on the penultimate syllables'). sources.quote: En arabe marocain, les séquences phoniques de type CVC connaissent un allongement significatif de la voyelle interconsonantique. Ce phénomène semble contredire la tendance relevée dans la littérature et qui consiste à réduire la durée du noyau vocalique en syllabe fermée. Cette étude phonétique et phonologique nous permet d'expliciter et de comprendre les fondements prosodiques de ce phénomène. [Transl.: In Moroccan Arabic, CVC phonic sequences show a significant lengthening of the inter-consonantal vowel. This seems to contradict the tendency noted in the literature to shorten the vowel nucleus in closed syllables. This phonetic and phonological study lets us make explicit and understand the prosodic bases of this phenomenon.]
sources.locator: Languages and Linguistics issue 12 contents page, abstract of pp. 1-12
sources.note: The abstract says nothing about where stress falls; it is a phonetic/phonological study of vowel lengthening in CVC sequences and their syllabic status. It bears indirectly on the catalog's weight class (CVC = heavy per Boudlal/Benkirane 1998): Maas 2019 (Skript Teil 1, p. 214 fn.) reports that Benkirane (1982; 2003) analyses such CVC sequences as open syllables with a loosely adjoined consonant. Silent on the catalog's stress coding. Low priority: the same author's 1998 Intonation Systems chapter (already on the list of works to obtain) is the stress statement of record.
